news.title: Students From Swing States Share Post-Election Reactions
news.description: After Democrats regained control of both Congressional houses in the 2026 midterm elections, Cornell students hailing from states where Democrats flipped Senate seats expressed shock, pride and excitement about the implications for their home states. In what election analysts have referred to as a "blue wave," Democrats flipped eight Republican-held Senate seats - in Kansas, Texas, Ohio, North Carolina, Iowa, South Carolina, Maine and Mississippi. While the Alaska Senate race has not yet been called, The New York Times predicts Mary Peltola (D) will flip the seat. Maine In Maine, former State Senator and logger Troy Jackson (D) defeated incumbent Sen. Susan Collins (R). Collins has served in the Senate since 1996 and was the only Republican senator to represent a state Kamala Harris won in the 2024 Presidential contest. Anna Siegel '28, who grew up in Yarmouth, Maine reflected on Collins' defeat after 30 years in the Senate. "I think there was a sense of pride that Maine was relevant and Maine was important … for the right reasons," Siegel told The Sun. Siegel explained that, prior to the 2026 midterms, Maine was "relevant because Susan Collins was one of the reasons Brett Kavanaugh was confirmed to the Supreme Court [which is] not a great thing to be known for." Jackson attacked Collins over her vote to confirm Justice Kavanaugh to the Supreme Court, arguing that this vote helped contribute to the overturning of Roe v Wade, the landmark case that had protected the federal right to abortion for half a century. Siegel maintained that Collins held a tight grip on Maine politics. "I was not daring to hope [that Jackson would win]," Siegel said. "Susan Collins has been my senator for more than my lifetime. … For my entire lifetime, it's just the way things are for me. It's the way things have been and will continue to be." Through her work with Main Youth for Climate Justice and the Sierra Club Siegel had lobbied Collins' office on several occasions. She also believes many Mainers historically backed Collins due to her role as Chair of the Appropriations Committee, which Collins argued helped bring increased funding back to Maine for infrastructure and state and local projects. After 30 years in the Senate, Siegel contends that Mainers have finally come to understand that Collins is not the very moderate Senator she portrays herself to be. "She had this bipartisan flair that she would flaunt a lot, and I think that resonated with a lot of Mainers," Siegel said. "And then, it became pretty clear in the last few years that that wasn't really true … [and] she was just falling into line behind President Trump." South Carolina In South Carolina, pediatrician Dr. Annie Andrews (D.) defeated incumbent Sen. Darline Graham (R), sending a South Carolinian Democrat to the Senate for the first time since 1998. Jessi Zheng '29, who grew up in what she called a "very red" small town near Myrtle Beach, South Carolina, recalled being "one of the only Asian people in [her] town." She characterized South Carolina as having a distinctly "red" identity and was "skeptical" that Andrews could win statewide. Zheng remembers how many people in South Carolina drove trucks that required large amounts of gas to operate. With the rising costs of gas, she told The Sun that she believes many voters grew disillusioned with the president and congressional Republicans. After former Senator Lindsay Graham (R-S.C.) died in July, South Carolina Governor Henry McMaster appointed Graham's sister, Darline, to complete his term in the Senate. President Donald Trump then endorsed Darline in her reelection bid. Zheng said that Darline's appointment to the Senate solely because her brother had held the position was seen to many in South Carolina as "an example of corruption and inequality." "Darlene Graham was definitely seen as a weak candidate because she has admitted to not knowing a lot about politics in the past," Zheng said. "That shows [her] lack of knowledge and [her] lack of qualification for this position." When asked a question about the United States' role in the South China Sea during a debate for the Republican nomination, Graham conceded that "national security is not my thing." On the other hand, Zheng felt that Andrews "really emphasized her family values" throughout the campaign. When Zheng heard that the election was called for Andrews, her first reaction was, "oh my god, I can't believe this is happening." Ohio Former Ohio Senator Sherrod Brown (D) ousted incumbent Jon Husted (R), who filled the vacancy of Vice President J.D. Vance's former seat. In the Governor's race, Amy Acton (D), former director of the Ohio Department of Health, defeated Vivek Ramaswamy (R), a former 2024 President candidate and billionaire biotech entrepreneur. Acton will be the first woman to hold the position in the state's history. Jenny Williams '27 paid close particular attention to the Governor's race in her home state. She thinks Acton's life story, as someone with an ordinary background, helped her eke out a victory in the race. "She's a normal person and she's really connected to Ohio," Williams said. By contrast, she pointed to Ramaswamy's net worth of $2.3 billion. Williams also views the Republican's "harsh" brand of politics as one of the reasons he "[pushed] people" away from his campaign. In particular, she highlighted a campaign advertisement that she viewed as distasteful. The ad featured Acton's mother, Donna Arthur, who called Acton a "liar," saying "my daughter needs help." Acton responded to the ad claiming she suffered from sexual abuse and neglect from her mother and stepfather, leading to Arthur losing custody of Acton and her brother. For Williams, the ad fit into a pattern of Republican politicians during the Trump era who are "disruptive," "outlandish with their remarks and unprofessional." Some Republicans in Ohio were swayed to vote for Democrat candidates for the first time in their lives, including Williams' father. "I was honestly surprised [by his vote]," she said, "but I was really happy." Texas In the Lone Star State, state representative and former middle school teacher James Talarico (D) defeated Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton (R) in the race for Senate, flipping the seat from red to blue. The last time a Democrat won a race for Senate in Texas was in 1988. In the race for governor, Texas State Representative Gina Hinojosa (D) defeated incumbent Governor Greg Abbott. Yosef Herrera '29 told The Sun that after last week's results, he feels his home state is no longer the "same Texas I was raised [in]." Herrera credited part of the leftward shift in Texas to "transplants," people who have moved from other states to Texas. "They're not born with those Texas values," he said. They're not strong in conservative beliefs like previous generations have been." Since 2020, Texas has seen more domestic migration than any other state in the nation, with 2.6 million people moving to the state. Herrera said that he is unsure what Texas' political future will look like amid an ideological shift. "We have people that are very much antithetical to a lot of the beliefs Texas was founded on," he said. Alex Blue-Baron '29 was following the races in her home state closely, texting friends at home for updates. When the Senate race was called for Talarico, Blue-Baron recalls seeing videos of crowds celebrating in the streets of Austin - "something that I never thought would happen," she said. Blue-Baron disputes the notion that Texas is a deeply red state and insists that these Democratic wins were a "long time coming." She argued that Texas' gerrymandered districts and low voter turnout, especially among Hispanic and Black communities, have prevented more Democrats from winning statewide in the past. Further, she said that many have been under the impression that their "vote doesn't matter because [the] state is so big." She also pointed to the large Democratic margin of victory in southern Texas, an area that has been "historically extremely, extremely red [and] went almost entirely blue in this election." "What we've seen in south Texas is this administration essentially bullying people living near the Rio Grande, pushing extremely aggressive border enforcement policies and threatening land seizures in our national parks," Blue-Baron wrote to The Sun. "People in the region are increasingly just fed up." After both Talarico's and Hinojosa's wins, Blue-Baron said that "for the first time in my life, I felt proud to be a Texan."

news.title: ‘Catch me if you can’: Dems launch probe into Trump’s 'vanity projects'
news.description: As President Donald Trump vows to redesign D.C. despite his historic 2026 midterm defeat, Congress is pushing back. Residents have also opposed Trump’s construction projects, including a monument and statue in his honor and the rebranding of the iconic Kimmel Center. Democrats promise to do what they can to stop and reverse Trump’s changes, calling them mere vanity projects. Trump’s administration boasts that his construction projects have added value to the District. One White House spokesperson, Davis Ingle, told NPR in an email that "no other president has done more to beautify our Nation's interior than President Trump." Ingle pointed to park cleanups, the Reflecting Pool, and the White House helipad and ballroom as examples, and said Democrats "should work with President Trump to make our nation's capital beautiful again." But Democrats and residents say Trump’s projects jeopardize and erase the cultural landscape of the District. Rep. Jared Huffman of California told NPR that the Trump administration has "played this game of Catch Me If You Can, where they roll ahead with the bulldozers and the tree cutters … and they wait for courts to shut them down." He says Democrats will use their congressional majority to challenge the administration. "There's no way that we could look away while these sacred, iconic places are being permanently changed in ways that violate the law and could have really terrible lasting impacts," Huffman added. He is the top Democrat on the House Natural Resources Committee, which has a legislative purview over public lands and national parks. Earlier this week, Huffman sent notices ordering administration officials and private companies to preserve their records for a future investigation, vowing to hold everyone accountable. "Whether it is the arch or … or the East Potomac golf course or any number of other examples around the United States capital, that is federal land, and we have a direct statutory responsibility to either authorize those changes or to stop them if they're proceeding without the proper authorization," Huffman said. There are several ways Democrats can enact the changes. They can pass laws to block specific projects. But with Trump vowing to “veto everything,” challenges may persist. However, there are other ways. "Legislation in principle is the cleanest way of doing it, but it's also not achievable," said David Super, who teaches administrative and constitutional law at Georgetown. "So what they're likely to do is cut off funds." The Constitution requires Congress to approve federal spending. However, Trump has not sought or received approval for projects such as the triumphal arch and White House ballroom, arguing that he does not need it. Rep. Chellie Pingree of Maine is the top Democrat on the House committee that oversees funding for the Interior Department. "Certainly Congress should have been involved, because we have the power of the purse," Pingree told NPR. "That is our ultimate tool. And Republicans have refused to use that. But we can use that in very many ways to block him or to use it for leverage." Pingree says Democrats could use their majority to draft spending bills that explicitly outline how federal funds can be used, while leaving open the possibility of suing the president if he ignores those restrictions. She also says Trump is igniting the fire further by not prioritizing what Americans are most concerned about, such as economic relief. That gives Democrats the upper hand. "They want the president to be focused on the issues they're dealing with: the cost of health care, the cost of food, the cost of gasoline," she said. news.title: Van Hollen takes on Schumer for majority leader after Democrats flip Senate
news.description: WASHINGTON (AP) — Democratic Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland said Thursday that he will run for Senate Majority Leader in the next Congress, setting up a challenge to Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer after the party swept to power in the midterm elections. Van Hollen said in a statement that “the American people called for change” and that is why he is running. “It’s now on us to meet this moment, and to do that we need new leadership,” Van Hollen said. “This is not about any one person — it’s about answering the call of the American people. That is why I’m running for Senate Majority Leader.” Van Hollen’s challenge comes after he said he was considering a bid and after Schumer has said he has the necessary support to win. The closed-door, secret-ballot election will be held in early December. The race will be the first contested election for Democratic leader in decades. The question of whether to reelect Schumer has already divided the caucus and many senators will not say publicly how they will vote. They have privately deliberated about what message to take from the election, and Schumer recruited many of the party’s winning candidates and raised money for them. Schumer has been talking to Democratic senators since the election and forming an agenda for 2027. In private caucus meetings this week, Schumer laid out a broad plan for their first 100 days in power. “I’m going to win it,” Schumer told The Associated Press in an interview last week. In a statement after Van Hollen’s announcement, Schumer said he welcomes any discussion about the future of the caucus. “I’m proud of what we’ve accomplished together — 55 seats and counting is an amazing result — and I have the votes to continue serving as Democratic Leader,” Schumer said. “I look forward to leading our new Democratic majority and delivering for the American people.” While Schumer is the favorite to win, Van Hollen’s run exposes a rift in the party that has put Schumer on the defensive since he sided with Republicans on a spending vote in March 2025. Even as he has redeemed himself within his caucus since then — leading them through a government shutdown last year and orchestrating huge wins in the election- many in the Democratic base are agitating for generational change. Van Hollen, 67, is not that much younger than Schumer, 75. But he has positioned himself as a new face in the party. He has also said he is considering a run for president. While most Democratic senators have either said they are supporting Schumer or are undecided, Van Hollen has at least one backer in next year’s caucus. Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan, who won a competitive election in his state last week, posted on X Thursday night that their majority will need “bold leadership.” “I called on Sen. @ChrisVanHollen to lead our caucus as a candidate back in April because he leads with courage and experience,” El-Sayed wrote. “We need both right now. Which is why I’m proud to stand with him in his bid to lead our Senate majority.” Several senators have said they are backing Schumer, including incoming Ohio Sen. Sherrod Brown, who beat Republican Sen. Jon Husted last week. Maine Sen. Angus King, an Independent who caucuses with Democrats and votes in the election, issued a statement after Van Hollen’s announcement: “Why would you fire the manager when you just won the World Series?” “Chuck Schumer is one of the principal architects of the most successful election in modern history, and I see no reason to change the leadership that helped make that success possible,” King wrote.
